entities.name: Paschal III
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Paschal III, born Guido of Crema, served as the second antipope to challenge the legitimate Pope Alexander III, reigning from 1164 until his death on September 27, 1168. His anti-papacy was a direct manifestation of the bitter power struggle between the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa and the Papacy, a continuation of the long-standing Investiture Controversy. Guido's election by a minority of cardinals and his subsequent consecration in Viterbo solidified a schism that deeply divided Latin Christendom and demonstrated the emperor's determination to assert secular control over ecclesiastical appointments and the very legitimacy of the pontiff.

Elevated after the death of Antipope Victor IV, Paschal III became a central figure in Frederick Barbarossa's persistent efforts to subjugate the Papacy and consolidate imperial authority across Italy and Germany. He was elected in Lucca and consecrated in Viterbo in 1164, immediately securing the emperor's endorsement. In 1167, Paschal III performed the controversial coronation of Frederick Barbarossa as Holy Roman Emperor in St. Peter's Basilica, an act intended to legitimize imperial power but which further deepened the schism. Despite his imperial backing, Paschal III struggled to gain widespread recognition among European monarchs and the clergy, with most states and ecclesiastical leaders ultimately aligning with Alexander III.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Paschal III's anti-papacy prolonged the significant papal schism of 1159-1177 for four crucial years, directly challenging the legitimate Pope Alexander III and serving as a key instrument of Frederick I Barbarossa's imperial ambitions to control the Church.
